title: Moths and rust (Matthew 6:19–21)
hookLine: where your treasure is, there your heart will be

cards: Open a drawer you haven't opened in years. The sweater you loved has holes in it. The gadget that cost a week's pay won't turn on.
The box of things you couldn't live without, you'd forgotten you had. Plenty of homes have a drawer like that.

It's a little funny, and a little sobering: things you once treasured, quietly falling apart while you weren't looking. Jesus's listeners had drawers like that too, and he starts a new part of the sermon right there.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal."
In his world, wealth could mean fine clothing, which moths could eat, and stored goods and metal, which could spoil and corrode.
The Greek word translated rust literally means eating: anything that eats away, corrosion or vermin.

teach.h: BREAK THROUGH: DIG THROUGH THE WALL.
teach.b: And break through is, in Greek, dig through: a burglar who doesn't pick the lock, he digs through the wall. Nothing on earth is completely safe.

Then the line that turns it all around: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Notice the order. You'd assume the heart leads and the money follows: I care about this, so I spend on it.
Jesus says it also works the other way.

teach.h: THERE WILL YOUR HEART BE ALSO.
teach.b: Put your treasure somewhere, and your heart goes after it. That's hopeful: if you want to care more about something, you can start by giving to it. So what are treasures in heaven?
Christians describe them as what moths can't eat: love given, mercy shown, the poor helped, time spent on what lasts. Read this way, Jesus isn't saying money doesn't matter.
Money is more like a compass, showing where your heart is heading. Your bank statement, you could say, is a kind of spiritual diary.

how: Some Christians give a regular share of their income to church and to the poor, often following the biblical tithe, and think of generosity as laying up treasure in heaven.

o: a book of words that mean the same thing
a hidden chest of gold buried for safekeeping
what you store up; your heart goes where it is

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.

s: the Greek word translated rust literally means eating
anything that eats away: corrosion or vermin.
Jesus says money doesn't matter at all

games.q: you want to care more about something good, but your heart isn't in it yet. what does this line suggest?
o: wait until you feel like it.
put your treasure there, and your heart will follow.
games.why: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." the heart follows the treasure.

practice: Picture where your money went this week, or open it up if you can, and read it like a diary, without judging yourself: what does it say you care about?
Notice one thing that surprises you, and one thing that lasts, a gift, a meal shared, a kindness. If you pray, you can offer both to God.

wordCard.voice: Treasure. What moths and rust eat away on earth, and what Jesus says to store instead in heaven, where nothing can touch it. Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

orig.note: Greek: treasure, storehouse. English thesaurus, a treasury of words, comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: where your treasure is. Your heart is never far behind. See you tomorrow.
